questions.question: Why do production audio generation models use neural audio codecs rather than operating directly on waveform samples?
options: Waveforms cannot be encoded with standard transformer positional embeddings
A 5-second clip at 16kHz is 80,000 samples; no transformer attends to sequences that long directly, so a codec compresses to 50-75 tokens/second before modeling
Waveform models require GPU hardware not available in cloud inference
Neural codecs improve audio quality by filtering out background noise before generation
questions.explanation: Transformers attending to raw 16kHz audio would face sequences of tens of thousands of elements per second. Neural codecs like Encodec and DAC compress waveforms to 50-75 discrete tokens per second using residual vector quantization, making sequence lengths tractable.

questions.question: What is Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) in a neural audio codec?
options: A single codebook that maps each audio frame to the nearest centroid
A cascade of K quantizers where each layer encodes the residual left by the previous layers, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction from multiple coarse-to-fine codebooks
A variational quantizer that replaces the continuous latent with a Gaussian approximation
A learned downsampling operation that reduces the sample rate by a factor of K
questions.explanation: RVQ uses K quantizer layers in sequence. Layer 1 quantizes the raw audio feature; layer 2 quantizes the residual (error) from layer 1; layer 3 quantizes the residual from layer 2; and so on. The decoder sums all K codebook embeddings to reconstruct the original with fidelity scaling in K.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which generative paradigm is preferred for text-to-speech in 2026 and why?
options: Latent diffusion, because it produces the highest audio quality without any iterative artifacts
Token-autoregressive modeling, because TTS is naturally causal and streams well, with each output token representing a short audio segment
GAN-based vocoders, because they have the lowest latency per output frame
Score-based SDE models, because they match the signal structure of speech better than discrete tokens
questions.explanation: TTS is causal by nature (left-to-right generation) and must stream to minimize time-to-first-audio. Codec AR models (VALL-E, ElevenLabs) generate tokens sequentially and stream immediately. Flow-matching models render a fixed clip length in one pass and cannot stream without chunking.

questions.question: What is the production throughput requirement for a streaming audio generation system and why?
options: The server must generate at least 1 token per second to avoid buffering
The server must generate at least 75 tokens per second per user to keep pace with playback at Encodec's 75 Hz token rate
The server must generate complete 5-second clips in under 100ms to avoid perceptible delay
The server must maintain a constant latency below the codec's frame size of 13ms
questions.explanation: Encodec produces 75 tokens per second of audio. A streaming server must generate tokens at least as fast as the user consumes them — 75 tokens/sec per user — or the audio buffer runs dry and playback stutters. This is the TPOT constraint for audio, analogous to decode speed for LLM text generation.

questions.question: What ethical risk is specifically called out for voice cloning models like VALL-E and XTTS?
options: Voice cloning models are limited to generating speech in the training language only
A 3-second voice sample is enough to clone a voice from a prompt, requiring abuse detection and opt-out lists in every production deployment
Voice cloning models cannot reproduce emotional prosody, making them unsuitable for professional use
Voice cloning requires retraining the full model for each new voice, making large-scale misuse impractical
questions.explanation: VALL-E, XTTS, and ElevenLabs can clone a voice from as little as 3 seconds of audio. This creates serious risks for impersonation, fraud, and non-consensual synthesis. The lesson explicitly flags that production models need abuse detection, speaker opt-out, and consent verification.

questions.question: MusicGen uses 'delayed parallel' decoding over multiple RVQ codebook streams. What problem does this solve?
options: It reduces the model size by sharing weights across the K codebook streams
It reduces the effective sequence length by generating K codebook levels with per-stream time offsets instead of flattening all K streams into a single sequence
It enables conditioning on midi note sequences rather than text prompts
It prevents posterior collapse in the RVQ codebook by decorrelating streams
questions.explanation: Naively flattening K codebook levels at 75 Hz produces K x 75 tokens per second. Delayed parallel decoding emits K streams with staggered offsets, keeping the effective sequence length at roughly 75 tokens/sec while still modeling all K residual levels, reducing transformer context length significantly.
